rationale: A wins because it turns the missing denominator into a real accountability story: `REI won't say how much of its business is used gear.` B has useful bones, especially `A record member payout while several stores see union drives`, but it leaves the used-gear disclosure problem as proof housekeeping instead of making it a pitchable angle. A gives the founder four genuinely different doors and tells them which ones bite back; B gives three good doors and leaves the sharpest one locked.
gaps_in_A: `REI won't say how much of its business is used gear` overstates the supplied fact. The update says the share is not disclosed; it does not prove REI refused to say.

`repair benches arrive at REI stores` may be visually useful, but it invents the store setup. The facts say repairs are available at stores, not that every store has benches or full-service repair capacity.
`a public retailer answering to shareholders has a hard time cheering on resale` is plausible analysis, not grounded in the update. It needs evidence or softer framing.
gaps_in_B: It misses the strongest accountability angle: the sustainability claim plus `share of sales from used gear not disclosed`. That is not a footnote; it is a story.
`online-plus-select-stores pilot` and `graduating resale/repair out of...pilot` invent pilot language. The update only says the program previously ran online and in select stores.
`competitors get benchmarked against` reaches past the fact set. No competitor behavior, market benchmark, or peer comparison was supplied.
`ongoing unionization activity` sharpens `has faced unionization activity` into a current-news claim. That needs current store-level proof before it goes anywhere.
